quran-affirms-torah-gospel: This is the foundation the whole section rests on, so it is worth getting straight. Muslims generally believe the Bible has been corrupted, which is why they do not accept it as evidence. But the Quran itself repeatedly speaks of the Torah and the Gospel as real, available guidance — and tells doubters to ask the people who were already reading them. That instruction only makes sense if those books could be trusted at the time it was given.
tahrif-doctrine-late-development: Tahrif is the Arabic word for corruption, and it is what Muslims mean when they say the Bible was changed. But there are two very different versions of the claim: that Jews and Christians misinterpret their scriptures, and that the actual written text was rewritten. This case traces which came first — and finds that the textual version was argued most influentially by Ibn Hazm, four centuries after Muhammad.
manuscripts-predate-muhammad: If the Bible was changed, the change has to have happened at some point in time — and manuscripts let us check. The Dead Sea Scrolls were copied around 150 BC, and complete Greek Bibles like Codex Sinaiticus around 350 AD. Both are centuries before Muhammad, and both match the Bible in use today. This case examines what that timing does to the corruption claim from either direction.
crucifixion-denial-vs-history: Quran 4:157 says the Jews did not kill Jesus and did not crucify him, but that it was made to appear so to them. That single verse is the sharpest disagreement between Islam and Christianity. It is also a historical claim, and the crucifixion is regarded by historians — including atheist ones — as among the best-attested facts about Jesus. This case sets the verse against the historical record.
quran-jesus-resume: Something surprising happens when you collect everything the Quran says about Jesus. He is born of a virgin, called the Messiah, described as sinless, gives life to the dead by God's permission, is a word from God and a spirit from him, is taken up alive, and returns at the end of the age. No other prophet in the Quran has anything like that record — including Muhammad, who is told to seek forgiveness for his sin.
gospel-judgment-test: Quran 5:47 tells the people of the Gospel to judge by what God revealed in it, and 10:94 tells anyone in doubt to ask those who were reading the Scripture before. Those are instructions, not observations, and they set a test. This case is about what happens when a Christian takes them up: the Quran itself has given permission to open the Gospel and read.
uthman-burning-companion-codices: About twenty years after Muhammad's death, the caliph Uthman found Muslims in different regions reciting the Quran differently. He commissioned one official version and ordered every other copy burned. That episode is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, Islam's most authoritative hadith collection — not by critics. This case examines what it means for a text's transmission history that the alternatives were destroyed.
sanaa-palimpsest-qiraat: In 1972 workers in the Great Mosque of Sanaa, Yemen, found a cache of old Quran manuscripts. One had been scraped clean and written over. Modern imaging recovered the erased lower layer — and it differs from the standard text in word order and wording. Alongside it sit the ten canonical qira'at, the recognized variant recitations. This case examines both together.
trinity-father-jesus-mary: Quran 5:116 has God ask Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods besides God. That has led many Muslims to believe Christians worship a trinity of Father, Jesus and Mary — which no Christian church has ever taught. This case examines what the verse says, how classical commentators read it, and why the misunderstanding matters for every conversation about the Trinity.
trinity-third-of-three: Quran 5:73 condemns those who say God is 'the third of three.' Christians agree with the condemnation, because the phrase describes three separate gods — which is tritheism, a heresy the church has always rejected. The Trinity is one God existing eternally as three persons. This case is about a real and important disagreement being fought over a position nobody on the Christian side holds.
begets-consort-carnal-sonship: Surah 112 says God 'neither begets nor is begotten,' and other verses ask how God could have a son when he has no consort. That reasoning assumes sonship means physical reproduction. Christian teaching has never held that: the Son is eternally begotten, not produced by a union. This case examines a rejection aimed at a doctrine Christians do not teach, and what a Christian should do about it.
god-is-love-monad: The Quran calls God al-Wadud, the loving. The New Testament goes further and says God is love. This case examines whether that difference is more than emphasis: love requires someone to love, so a God who is love in his own nature needs relationship within himself — which is what the Trinity describes, and which a strictly solitary God cannot have before creation.
best-of-deceivers: Several Quranic verses call God khayru al-makirin, usually translated 'the best of planners' but built on a root that carries deception. This case handles it carefully in both directions: Christians often overstate it into 'Allah is a deceiver,' which is unfair to how Arabic works, while the classical commentaries do discuss divine deception of God's enemies in ways worth examining honestly.
word-and-spirit-titles: Quran 4:171 calls Jesus God's word which he cast into Mary, and a spirit from him. These are extraordinary titles, given to no one else in the Quran, in a verse whose whole purpose is to deny that Jesus is divine. This case examines the tension inside a single verse — and how to raise it as a question rather than a gotcha.
clay-birds-apocrypha: Quran 3:49 describes Jesus making birds out of clay and breathing life into them. That story is not in any Gospel. It appears in the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, a second-century apocryphal text that the church rejected as legendary. This case examines what it means that a story circulating as folklore turns up in the Quran presented as history.
son-of-god-divine-claims: Much of the Quran's argument against Christianity targets 'son of God' understood as physical offspring. Meanwhile the specific claims that actually led to Jesus being charged with blasphemy — forgiving sins, claiming to be before Abraham, accepting worship — are never addressed. This case examines what the Quran engages and what it leaves untouched.
quran-never-quotes-scriptures: The Quran repeatedly says it confirms the Torah and the Gospel that came before it. What it does not do is quote them. There is no passage where it cites a line of Isaiah or a verse of Matthew and says: this is what I am confirming. This case examines that absence and what it suggests about the relationship being claimed.
injil-problem: Islam teaches that Jesus received a book called the Injil — a single revealed Gospel, now lost or corrupted. The Gospels we have are four accounts written about Jesus by others, not a book given to him. No manuscript, quotation or ancient reference to a separate Injil has ever been found. This case examines a claim about a document that leaves no trace anywhere.
sun-muddy-spring: Quran 18:86 describes Dhul-Qarnayn travelling west until he found the sun setting in a spring of murky water. Modern defenders read it as describing an appearance from the traveller's viewpoint. This case is careful with that defense — it is a real possibility — but it also examines what the classical commentators, including al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understood the verse to mean.
reproductive-science-galen: Quran 86:5–7 says man is created from a fluid issuing from between the backbone and the ribs, and 23:14 describes a sequence from clot to lump to bones which are then clothed with flesh. Both track the medical understanding of the Greek physician Galen, current in the region at the time. This case examines the claim that the Quran's embryology is miraculously ahead of its era.
mary-sister-of-aaron: Quran 19:28 has Mary addressed as 'sister of Aaron,' and 66:12 calls her 'daughter of Imran' — Imran being the Quranic name for the father of Moses and Aaron, who lived over a thousand years earlier. Muslims from Najran raised this with Muhammad in his own lifetime. This case examines both the objection and the traditional answer that these are honorific, not literal, family terms.
samaritan-anachronism: Quran 20:85–97 says a figure called al-Samiri — the Samaritan — led Israel into making the golden calf. The Samaritans as a people emerged from the region of Samaria, which was named centuries after the Exodus and populated after the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC. This case examines the anachronism and the alternative etymologies proposed for the word.
dhul-qarnayn-alexander: Quran 18:83–102 tells of Dhul-Qarnayn, 'the two-horned one,' travelling to the ends of the earth and building a barrier against Gog and Magog. A Syriac Christian legend about Alexander the Great, containing the same episodes in the same order, circulated in the region shortly before. This case examines the relationship between the two texts.
cosmology-stars-missiles: Quran 67:5 says God adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and made them missiles to drive away devils. Other verses describe seven heavens and a sky held up without visible pillars. This case examines the picture of the universe the text assumes, and treats the modern reinterpretations fairly rather than dismissing them.
abrogation-satanic-verses: Quran 2:106 says that when God abrogates a verse he brings a better one — the basis for naskh, where later revelation cancels earlier. Alongside it sits the incident reported by early historians in which Muhammad recited verses praising three pagan goddesses and later withdrew them as satanic. This case examines both together, since both concern revelation being replaced.
compilation-lost-verses: The Quran was not written as a single book during Muhammad's lifetime. Early Islamic sources describe it being gathered after his death from palm stalks, stones and the memories of reciters — after many memorizers died at the battle of Yamama. The same sources record verses that companions remembered but which never made the final text. This case works entirely from those Islamic accounts.
uthman-standardization-qiraat: This case follows the transmission story to the present day. After Uthman's standardization and burning of variant copies, ten canonical readings remained recognized. Two are in print now: the Hafs reading, used almost everywhere, and Warsh, used across North and West Africa. They differ in wording in places. This case examines what that means for the claim of a single perfectly preserved text.
aisha-age: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the two most authoritative hadith collections in Sunni Islam — record that Muhammad married Aisha when she was six and consummated the marriage when she was nine. This is not an accusation from outside; it is reported in Islam's own most trusted sources, and Aisha is one of Islam's most important narrators. This case handles it with the care it needs.
women-and-captives: Quran 4:34 instructs husbands, as a final step with a rebellious wife, to strike her — translations differ on how strongly. Quran 4:24 and the hadith address sexual relations with women captured in war. These are difficult texts, and this case presents the range of Muslim interpretations, including the modernist readings, before examining them.
zaynab-hastening-revelation: Zaynab was married to Zayd, Muhammad's adopted son. After their divorce, Quran 33:37 sanctioned Muhammad's marriage to her and set aside the Arabian rule that an adopted son's wife was off limits. Aisha is recorded in the hadith saying she felt God hastened to fulfil his desires. This case examines a revelation that resolves the messenger's personal situation.
prophet-test-signs: Deuteronomy 18:22 gives a public test for a prophet: what he predicts must happen. This case applies that test to Muhammad and finds an unusual situation — the Quran does not present him as making predictive prophecies or performing miracles, and says explicitly that the Quran itself is his sign. The case examines that claim on its own terms rather than demanding what was never offered.
aorta-test: Quran 69:44–46 says that if the messenger had invented sayings and attributed them to God, God would have seized him and cut his life-artery. The hadith record that after eating poisoned meat at Khaybar, Muhammad said in his final illness that he felt his aorta being cut. This case sets the verse beside the report and examines both, including the traditional interpretations.
salvation-scales: Islam pictures judgment as a scale weighing a person's good deeds against their bad. There is no assurance built into the system, and the hadith record Muhammad himself saying he did not know what would be done with him. Christianity offers the opposite — a righteousness credited rather than earned, and a stated ground for assurance. This case examines the difference at the level a person actually feels it.
taqiyya-deception: Taqiyya is a real concept: concealing your faith under threat of persecution. It is primarily a Shia doctrine, developed by a persecuted minority. In Western polemic it has been inflated into a general licence for Muslims to lie to non-Muslims, which is false. This case explains what the doctrine actually is and does — and then examines the narrower questions that are legitimate.
sharia-apostasy-jizya: Classical Islamic jurisprudence prescribes death for apostasy, a poll tax called jizya for Jews and Christians under Muslim rule, and fixed corporal punishments known as hudud. This case works from the classical legal manuals rather than from headlines, and is careful to note how much of it is applied anywhere today and how much modern Muslims reject.
allah-moon-god: The claim that Allah was originally a pre-Islamic moon god circulates widely in Christian material, usually with a picture of a crescent. It does not survive examination: 'Allah' is simply the Arabic word for God, used by Arabic-speaking Christians before Islam existed and still today. This case explains the archaeological argument behind it and why it fails.
quran-late-composition: Some revisionist scholars have argued the Quran was assembled long after Muhammad. The manuscript evidence does not support it — the Birmingham folios and the Sanaa manuscripts both date to the seventh century. This case exists because getting this right cuts both ways: it removes a bad Christian argument, and it establishes the same manuscript standard the Bible is judged by.
spread-only-by-sword: 'Islam spread only by the sword' is a caricature. Conquest did establish Muslim rule rapidly, but conversion of populations was often slow and driven by tax status, trade and intermarriage — and much of Islam's spread into Indonesia and West Africa was through merchants. This case gives the honest picture, which is more complicated and more useful.
inheritance-math-awl: Quran 4:11–12 sets fixed inheritance shares for various relatives. In some family combinations the fractions add up to more than the whole estate — a mathematical result, not a matter of opinion. Islamic jurisprudence developed a doctrine called awl to reduce all shares proportionally. This case examines the arithmetic and the fix devised for it.
banu-qurayza-massacre: After the Battle of the Trench in 627, the Jewish tribe of Banu Qurayza surrendered. The men — between 600 and 900 by the traditional sources — were executed and the women and children enslaved. The judgment was pronounced by an arbitrator and endorsed by Muhammad. This case works entirely from Islam's own earliest biographies, and explains the context of the siege.
muhammad-in-the-bible: Muslim outreach often argues that the Bible predicts Muhammad, using three passages: the prophet like Moses in Deuteronomy 18, the Paraclete in John 14–16, and 'altogether lovely' in Song of Songs 5:16, said to be his name. This case works through each in context, including why the Song of Songs argument depends on a Hebrew word used elsewhere of plundered treasures.
ishmael-covenant-kaaba: The Bible traces the covenant through Isaac, saying so explicitly while also promising blessing to Ishmael. Islam holds that Abraham and Ishmael built the Kaaba in Mecca and that the son nearly sacrificed was Ishmael — although the Quran does not name him. This case compares the two accounts and examines where the tradition, rather than the text, supplies the details.
quran-borrowed-legends: Several Quranic passages closely match Jewish and Christian stories circulating in the region — the principle that killing one soul is like killing all mankind, which appears in the Mishnah as a rabbi's commentary; the Seven Sleepers, a Christian legend; and Abraham thrown into a furnace, from a Jewish midrash. This case examines material that appears in the Quran as God's own speech.
houris-material-paradise: The Quran describes paradise with gardens, rivers, couches, and companions called houris — and the hadith add considerable detail. Christian teaching describes heaven as the presence of God, with Jesus saying there is no marriage there. This case compares the two pictures without the crude version of the argument, and examines what each says about the goal of the religion.
women-testimony-inheritance: Quran 2:282 asks for two male witnesses, or one man and two women, for a debt contract; 4:11 gives a daughter half a son's inheritance share. This case presents the texts, the traditional reasoning behind them, and the modern Muslim interpretations that read them as context-specific — and examines them without pretending the question is simple in either direction.
fatiha-daily-prayer-jews-christians: The Fatiha is the opening chapter of the Quran and is recited in every unit of the five daily prayers — around seventeen times a day. It ends by asking not to be led down the path of those who earned wrath, nor of those who went astray. Classical commentary identifies those two groups as the Jews and the Christians. This case examines the text and that traditional reading.
hadith-chain-of-custody: Most of Islamic practice comes from the hadith rather than the Quran, and the hadith were compiled 150 to 250 years after Muhammad's death. Islamic scholarship developed a rigorous science for grading them by their chains of narrators. This case examines that system honestly — its real strengths and the problem al-Bukhari himself faced in rejecting the overwhelming majority of what he collected.
mariya-hafsa-surah-66: Surah 66 opens by asking Muhammad why he forbids himself what God has made lawful in order to please his wives, and releases him from an oath. The traditional accounts behind it involve his wives Hafsa and Aisha and a woman named Mariya. This case sets out the reported incident, the range of versions, and the question of a revelation that resolves a domestic dispute.
safiyya-khaybar-marriage: Safiyya was a Jewish noblewoman of Khaybar. In the campaign there, her husband was killed and she was taken captive; Muhammad married her, according to the sources, within days. This case works from the Islamic biographies, and presents the traditional defense — that marriage conferred status and freedom — alongside the plain sequence of events.
mutah-temporary-marriage: Mut'ah is a fixed-term marriage contracted for a set period. The hadith record that Muhammad permitted it, and Sunni and Shia Islam disagree sharply about whether it was later forbidden — Shia jurisprudence still permits it. This case examines the practice, the disagreement, and the questions it raises about the nature of marriage.
kaaba-black-stone-pagan-rites: Before Islam the Kaaba was a shrine housing many idols, and pilgrims already circled it, kissed the Black Stone, ran between the hills of Safa and Marwa, and threw stones at pillars. Muhammad cleansed the shrine of idols and kept the rites. This case examines the continuity, and is careful to separate it from the false claim that Muslims worship the stone.
sword-verses-final-command: The Quran contains both conciliatory verses and militant ones, and because it is not arranged chronologically, the order matters enormously. Surah 9 is among the last revealed, and includes the verses about fighting the idolaters and the People of the Book. Under the doctrine of abrogation, later cancels earlier. This case examines the chronology question that decides how the whole book reads.
muhammad-bewitched: Sahih al-Bukhari records that a Jewish man cast a spell on Muhammad such that he would imagine he had done things he had not — lasting, in some reports, for months. This case examines what that report, from Islam's most trusted collection, raises about the period of revelation, and presents the traditional responses, which distinguish personal affairs from prophetic transmission.
sins-cast-on-jews-christians: Sahih Muslim contains a report that on the Day of Judgment every Muslim will be given a Jew or a Christian and told: this is your ransom from the Fire. This case examines the hadith, its grading, the discomfort many Muslims express about it, and the way it inverts the Christian idea of substitution — where the innocent bears the guilty's penalty voluntarily.
uzair-son-of-god: Quran 9:30 says the Jews claim Ezra is the son of God, paired with the Christian claim about Jesus. No Jewish group in history is known to have taught this. This case examines the verse, the various scholarly attempts to identify a sect that might have held such a view, and what it means for a text describing another religion's beliefs.
allah-name-polemic: Some Christian material argues that because Muslims call God 'Allah,' they worship a different deity with a pagan name. Arabic-speaking Christians have always used the word, it appears in Arabic Bibles, and it is simply the Arabic for God. This case explains why the argument fails and redirects to the real question — not what God is called, but what is claimed about him.
first-revelation-terror: The account of the first revelation in Sahih al-Bukhari is more unsettling than most people expect. Muhammad is squeezed by a being in the cave, flees home shaking and asks to be covered, fears for himself, and — in some reports — considers throwing himself from a cliff. He is reassured by his wife Khadija and by her Christian cousin Waraqa. This case examines the earliest account as it stands.
quran-262-vs-385: Quran 2:62 appears to promise reward to Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the Last Day and do good. Quran 3:85 says that whoever seeks a religion other than Islam will not have it accepted. These pull in opposite directions, and the classical resolution is that 3:85 abrogates 2:62. This case examines both verses and the interpretive history.
slavery-never-abolished: The Quran and hadith regulate slavery extensively — encouraging manumission as a virtue, setting rules for treatment — but never abolish it. Slavery persisted in Muslim societies into the twentieth century and was ended largely under external pressure. This case examines the record fairly, noting that Christian scriptures also regulate rather than abolish it, which is a point Muslims rightly raise.
fgm-classical-fiqh: Female circumcision is discussed in classical Islamic jurisprudence, with the schools ranging from recommending it to treating it as obligatory. The main supporting hadith is graded weak by many scholars. This case is deliberately careful: the chains are weak, the practice is regional rather than universal in Islam, and overstating it is both wrong and counterproductive.
quran-grammar-irregularities: The Quran presents its own eloquence as its central miracle, and challenges anyone to produce a chapter like it. Grammarians — including classical Muslim ones — have catalogued passages where the case endings, gender agreement or number do not follow standard Arabic. This case examines those passages and the traditional explanations for them.
quran-65-4-child-iddah: Quran 65:4 sets the waiting period after divorce for women, and specifies a period for 'those who have not yet menstruated.' Classical commentators read this as covering girls too young to have begun menstruating. This case examines the verse, the classical commentary, and the modern interpretations that read it as referring to women with irregular cycles.
four-witnesses-rape-standard: Quran 24:4 requires four witnesses to establish the charge of unlawful intercourse, on pain of flogging the accuser. That standard was designed to protect women from slander. In several modern legal systems it has been applied to rape cases, meaning a woman who cannot produce four witnesses risks being charged herself. This case examines both the original intent and the modern application.
iblis-angel-or-jinn: Quran 18:50 says Iblis was one of the jinn. Elsewhere the command to bow to Adam is given to the angels, and Iblis is described as being among them and refusing — using a grammatical construction that normally marks an exception from the group just named. This case examines whether the sentence works if Iblis was never an angel.
creation-six-or-eight-days: The Quran says repeatedly that God created the heavens and the earth in six days. Surah 41:9–12 then breaks the creation into stages with day-counts attached — two, four, and two — which add to eight. This case examines the arithmetic and the traditional reading that the four-day period includes the first two.
qadar-created-for-hell: Qadar is the Islamic doctrine of divine decree. Quran 7:179 says God has created many jinn and men for Hell. This case examines that verse alongside the Christian debate over predestination, which is a real and unresolved argument inside Christianity too — and is honest that both traditions have hard things to say here.
triple-talaq-halala: A husband may divorce by pronouncement, and after the third pronouncement the divorce is final. Quran 2:230 then says the couple cannot remarry unless she marries another man and that marriage also ends. This has produced the practice of halala, a temporary intervening marriage arranged so a couple can reunite. This case examines the rule and the practice it generates.
surah-9-missing-basmala: Every chapter of the Quran but one opens with the basmala — 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate.' Surah 9 does not. Early Islamic sources record that the companions were uncertain whether Surah 9 was a separate chapter or the continuation of Surah 8, and Uthman made a judgment call. This case examines that reported editorial decision.
haman-in-pharaohs-egypt: The Quran places a figure named Haman at Pharaoh's court in Egypt, building a tower. Haman is the villain of the biblical book of Esther, set in Persia roughly a thousand years later. This case examines the identification, and gives a fair hearing to the argument that the name reflects an Egyptian title rather than the Persian official.
prophetic-medicine-science-test: Muslim outreach often argues that the Quran contains scientific knowledge ahead of its time. That argument sets a standard, so this case applies the same standard to the medical hadith — dipping a fallen fly in your drink because one wing carries disease and the other the cure, drinking camel urine as medicine, and black seed as a remedy for everything but death.
adam-sixty-cubits: Sahih al-Bukhari records Muhammad saying that God created Adam sixty cubits tall — about ninety feet — and that people have been getting shorter ever since. This case examines the hadith, its grading as sound, and the archaeological record of human height, which shows no such decline. It also examines how modern Muslim scholars handle sound hadith that appear factually wrong.
aisha-was-19-revisionism: In recent decades some Muslim writers have argued Aisha was actually eighteen or nineteen, reconstructing her age from the ages of relatives and the dates of events. This case takes the argument seriously and examines it — and notes that mainstream Sunni scholarship, including the major fatwa bodies, rejects it and continues to affirm the hadith as they stand.
avoid-muhammad-never-existed: A small group of revisionist scholars has argued Muhammad is legendary. Almost no historian agrees: the evidence for his existence includes early non-Muslim sources, coins, inscriptions and the Dome of the Rock. This case exists because using this claim destroys your credibility on everything else — and because the manuscript standard involved is the same one that supports the Bible.
avoid-petra-qibla: Dan Gibson has argued from mosque orientations that the earliest qibla pointed to Petra rather than Mecca. The claim has attracted attention online but has not persuaded specialists, and early mosque orientation is affected by practical factors like available survey knowledge. This case explains why it is not a hill to fight on.
avoid-black-stone-worship-slogan: Muslims kiss the Black Stone during pilgrimage, and it is a pre-Islamic element retained — which is a legitimate topic. But saying Muslims worship it is false: the caliph Umar is recorded saying plainly that it is only a stone that can neither harm nor benefit. This case explains the distinction and how to raise the real question.
avoid-26-different-qurans: Screenshots circulate claiming there are 26 or 31 different Qurans. The real situation is that ten canonical readings are recognized and two are in print, differing in vowels and occasionally consonants — which is a serious and documented point. The inflated number invites an easy correction. This case explains what the accurate version is and why it is stronger.
avoid-taqiyya-overclaim: Taqiyya is a real doctrine about concealing faith under persecution, primarily Shia. The claim that all Muslims are commanded to lie to non-Muslims is false, and using it tells your friend you have absorbed material about them rather than learned anything. This case gives the accurate account and shows where the narrower legitimate questions lie.
avoid-72-virgins-in-quran: The number 72 is not in the Quran. It comes from a hadith graded as good rather than sound, in the collection of al-Tirmidhi. The Quran does describe companions in paradise, which is a fair subject. This case exists because leading with a number your friend can immediately tell you is not in their scripture ends the conversation on the spot.
